facts.F1: The Applicant is a national of India who entered Hong Kong illegally on 8 October 2014 and was arrested by police on 2 November 2014.
facts.F2: The Applicant raised a claim for non-refoulement protection by way of a written representation on 4 November 2014.
facts.F3: He failed to report to the Immigration Department until 21 April 2015 and was released on recognizance on 24 November 2014.
facts.F4: On 9 June 2015 he requested to cancel his non-refoulement claim, which was accepted by the Immigration Department.
facts.F5: On 31 July 2015 the Applicant requested to re-open his claim, which was accepted by the Immigration Department.
facts.F6: The Applicant attended a briefing by the Immigration Department for the commencement of the screening process of his claim with the assistance of an interpreter on 17 June 2016.
facts.F7: He was given a notice of the requirements for him to substantiate his claim together with a blank Non-refoulement Claim Form (NCF) with a stipulation to return its completed form within 28 days.
facts.F8: The Applicant failed to return his NCF by 5 August 2016 or at any time thereafter.
facts.F9: On 15 August 2016 the Immigration Department informed the Applicant that his claim was treated as withdrawn.
facts.F10: The Applicant provided information in support of his request to re-open his claim under section 37ZG(3) of the Ordinance on 19 October 2016, but the Director refused his request on 4 November 2016.
facts.F11: The Applicant lodged his appeal to the Torture Claims Appeal Board against the Director's decision on 16 November 2016, which was dismissed on 8 September 2017.
facts.F12: The Applicant's conduct in relation to his claim since 2014 shows that he failed to provide any cogent evidence to satisfy the statutory requirement.
facts.F13: There was a substantial and excessive delay in the Applicant's application for leave for which there was no good reason.

facts.F1: The Applicant is a 27-year-old national of Pakistan who entered Hong Kong illegally on 10 September 2020.
facts.F2: He was arrested by police on 15 September 2020 and raised a non-refoulement claim on the basis that if he returned to Pakistan he, as a Shia Muslim, would be harmed or killed by some local Sunni Muslims in his home village over their religious dispute.
facts.F3: The Applicant was born and raised as a Shia Muslim in Tehsil & District Nankana, Punjab Province, Pakistan.
facts.F4: After leaving school, he worked as a shopkeeper in his home village and, together with his fellow Shias, regularly worshipped in the village mosque.
facts.F5: In October 2016, the Applicant organized a religious seminar in his home village for Shia Muslims, which led to confrontations with Sunni villagers.
facts.F6: The Applicant continued to organize religious gatherings, despite warnings from Sunni villagers, which led to violent confrontations in 2016 and 2018.
facts.F7: In December 2018, the Applicant was ambushed and attacked by a group of Sunnis, suffering cuts and bruises.
facts.F8: The Applicant fled to his uncle's place in Morkunda Town in District Sheikupura, but after a gun shot was fired at him in the local market in April 2019, he departed for China and later sneaked into Hong Kong.
facts.F9: The Applicant raised a non-refoulement claim and completed a Non-refoulement Claim Form on 7 June 2021, attending a screening interview before the Immigration Department with legal representation.
facts.F10: The Director of Immigration rejected the Applicant's claim on all applicable grounds, including risk of torture, risk of absolute or non-derogable rights being violated, and risk of persecution.
facts.F11: The Applicant lodged an appeal to the Torture Claims Appeal Board, which was dismissed on 10 December 2021.
facts.F12: The Applicant filed his Form 86 for leave to apply for judicial review of the Board's decision on 5 January 2022.
facts.F13: The Applicant has since submitted an affirmation stating that his problem has been resolved and that he wants to return to his home country.

lawsuit_type: Application for Leave to Apply for Judicial Review
reference_issues: Whether the Applicant has established a reasonably arguable basis for his intended challenge.
Whether the Director of Immigration and the Torture Claims Appeal Board erred in law or acted irrationally in their decisions.

facts.F2: She was arrested by police on 18 November 2011 for theft and was subsequently convicted and sentenced to prison for 12 months.

facts.F4: The Applicant was born and raised in Ducot Vcab, Itogon Benguet, the Philippines, and was actively involved in her community work and became one of the community leaders before leaving for Hong Kong.
facts.F5: In 2010, the local village head EM asked her to help him get re-elected, but she refused due to his corrupt practices, and he blamed her for his loss and made threats against her.
facts.F6: The Applicant made arrangements to leave the Philippines by applying to work as a foreign domestic helper in Hong Kong.
facts.F7: She filed a Supplementary Claim Form (SCF) on 3 December 2015 and attended a screening interview before the Immigration Department with legal representation from the Duty Lawyer Service (DLS).
facts.F8: The Director of Immigration rejected her claim on all grounds other than torture risk on 27 January 2016.
facts.F9: The Applicant appealed to the Torture Claims Appeal Board (Board) against the Director's decision and attended an oral hearing on 5 July 2018, during which she claimed to be suffering from breast cancer and feared she would not receive medical treatment in her home country.
facts.F10: The Board dismissed her appeal on 20 August 2018, finding inconsistencies and discrepancies in her evidence and doubting her claim of fear of harm from EM.
facts.F11: The Applicant filed her Form 86 for leave to apply for judicial review of the Board's decision on 26 November 2018, but was six days late with her application.
facts.F12: The Court granted an extension of time for the Applicant’s late Notice of Application for Leave to Apply for Judicial Review.

facts.F1: The Applicant arrived in Hong Kong on 27 May 2016 with permission to remain as a visitor until 10 June 2016, but overstayed and was arrested by police on 5 August 2016.
facts.F2: He raised a non-refoulement claim on the basis that if he returned to Pakistan, he would be harmed or killed by his brother and his brothers-in-law over family disputes.
facts.F3: The Applicant was born and raised in Sialkot City, Punjab, Pakistan, and has a history of conflict with his brother Adnan, who has physically and emotionally harmed him on multiple occasions.
facts.F4: In 2009, Adnan married a girl whose family had close connections with the political party Pakistan Muslim League (N), and he became a supporter of that party.
facts.F5: The Applicant took a trip to Dubai in 2014 and left Adnan in charge of his business, but upon his return, he discovered that Adnan had withdrawn all the money from the business accounts.
facts.F6: The Applicant and Adnan had a heated argument, and Adnan and his in-laws attacked the Applicant with punches and wooden sticks.
facts.F7: The Applicant was arrested by the police but released without charge; he then started receiving threatening phone calls from unknown numbers, prompting him to flee to Lahore and then Islamabad.
facts.F8: The Applicant's father intervened and transferred the family house to the Applicant, but he continued to receive death threats, and eventually fled to Hong Kong.
facts.F9: The Director of Immigration rejected the Applicant's non-refoulement claim on all applicable grounds, including risk of torture, risk of violation of absolute or non-derogable rights under the Hong Kong Bill of Rights, and risk of persecution.
facts.F10: The Torture Claims Appeal Board dismissed the Applicant's appeal, finding inconsistencies and discrepancies in his account of events and concluding that state and police protection, as well as internal relocation, were available to him in Pakistan.
facts.F11: The Applicant failed to provide any grounds for his intended application and did not show any error in law or procedural unfairness in the Board's decision.

facts.F1: The applicant, a national of Bangladesh, entered Hong Kong illegally on 27 February 2007 and was arrested by the police for being an illegal immigrant on 25 September 2007.
facts.F2: On 20 May 2008, he lodged a torture claim which was later taken as a non-refoulement claim under the unified screening mechanism.
facts.F3: His claim was based on the risk of being harmed or killed by Hasina’s relatives and members of the Awami League (AL) if he is refouled.
facts.F4: The applicant claimed that he was forced to marry Hasina against his will and later escaped to another village in Dhaka.
facts.F5: In 1994, he was arrested by the police for refusing to honor the marriage and was later bailed out.
facts.F6: He then moved to Dhaka but was informed that Hasina’s relatives reopened the cases against him and an arrest warrant was issued.
facts.F7: The applicant also claimed to have assisted the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) in the election against the AL and was confronted and assaulted by AL members.
facts.F8: He fled to Hong Kong in 2006 for protection.
facts.F9: The Director of Immigration considered the applicant’s claim in relation to the risks of torture, violation of the right to life, torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, and persecution.
facts.F10: The Director dismissed the applicant’s claim, finding that the level of risk of harm upon refoulement was low and state protection would be available to him.
facts.F11: The applicant appealed to the Torture Claims Appeal Board which also dismissed his claim, finding that the applicant’s claim was illogical and implausible and state protection and internal relocation were viable alternatives.
facts.F12: The applicant was not given legal advice by his duty lawyer and did not receive translation services for the hearing bundle and the Board’s Decision.
facts.F13: The Court considered the length of the delay, the reasons for the delay, the prospect of the intended application and the prejudice to the putative respondent in deciding whether to grant an extension of time.
facts.F14: Interpreter services were provided at hearings for the applicant.
facts.F15: No valid grounds were raised by the applicant to challenge the Board’s Decision.

facts.F1: The applicant is a national of Pakistan who entered Hong Kong illegally on 22 September 2006 and was arrested by the police on 5 October 2006.

facts.F3: The applicant's application to reopen his torture claim was denied.
facts.F4: On 11 November 2013, he lodged a claim for Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CIDTP).
facts.F5: The applicant based his claim on the fear that, if refouled, he would be harmed or killed by his enemy Imamia Student Organization (ISO) from the Shia sect.
facts.F6: The applicant belonged to another organization called Sunni Terek Force (STF) under the Ahley Sunnat sect.
facts.F7: The two organizations had disputes over the place of worship.
facts.F8: In 2006, the applicant was promoted to be the vice president of STF.
facts.F9: Thereafter, the people from ISO constantly threatened to kill the applicant.
facts.F10: In a gathering held in March or April 2006, the applicant was almost shot by four gunmen from the ISO.
facts.F11: The report of the shooting incident to the police was of no avail as they were biased against the STF.
facts.F12: The applicant claimed that the STF filed two false charges against him to revenge against the charges laid against the STF members for offences including possession of firearms.
facts.F13: As a result, the applicant was detained by the police for two weeks and he was verbally abused.

facts.F1: The Applicant is a national of India, born in 1988, and arrived in Hong Kong in September 2014.
facts.F2: He overstayed in Hong Kong and was arrested on 7 March 2015, then released on recognizance and made a formal non-refoulement claim on 9 March 2015.
facts.F3: On 17 January 2018, the Applicant filed a Non-refoulement Claim Form under the unified screening mechanism to the Director, claiming he will be harmed by a loan shark 'Vicky' due to his inability to repay a loan and feared harm because of his Muslim religion.
facts.F4: The Director refused the Applicant’s application for non-refoulement protection by a Notice of Decision dated 9 February 2018.
facts.F5: The Applicant appealed to the Board against the decision of the Director and appeared before the Board at a hearing held on 29 October 2018.
facts.F6: The Board rejected the appeal by the Applicant and confirmed the decision of the Director by its decision given on 24 January 2019.
facts.F7: The Applicant was a Sunni Muslim born in Bihar state in India and had worked as a salesman in Khidderpore, Kolkata.
facts.F8: He commenced a mobile phone resale business in Kolkata in 2011, then borrowed money from a rich and influential member of the Bharatiya Janata Party named Vicky in 2013.
facts.F9: The Applicant decided to expand his business and Vicky trusted him so no agreement was signed, but Vicky demanded 25% share of the profits.
facts.F10: From the middle of 2013, Vicky demanded a greater share of the profits, but because business was poor, the Applicant could not make a profit, so Vicky threatened to kill him and his uncle for failing to share any profit and failing to repay the principal.
facts.F11: The Applicant came to Hong Kong and was told by his uncle to remain in Hong Kong as Vicky may harm him if he returned to India.
facts.F12: The Applicant overstayed in Hong Kong, fearing to return to India, and received a call from his parents that his uncle had been seriously injured by Vicky and framed by the police in a drug case due to Vicky’s influence.
facts.F13: After being arrested in Hong Kong for overstaying, the Applicant lodged his non-refoulement claim.
facts.F14: The Director found on the evidence that the risk of harm to the Applicant coming from Vicky to be low and that the Applicant, as a Muslim living in India, had never been harmed but that his fears only arose from what he has heard.
facts.F15: The Director further found from the Country of Origin Information ('COI') material that state protection and internal relocation to be available to the Applicant despite the Applicant’s beliefs otherwise.
facts.F16: On the evidence before the Board, the Board found that the Applicant’s claims regarding the loan from Vicky to be untruthful, and even if true, the Applicant’s problems relating thereto are confined to his home area.
facts.F17: The Board was not satisfied that there are substantial or strong grounds or a real risk that the Applicant will suffer harm due to his Muslim religion if returned to India.
facts.F18: The Board found the Applicant has failed to substantiate each of the applicable grounds under the USM in respect of his non-refoulement claim for protection.
facts.F19: The Board has given detailed and well-reasoned findings of fact rejecting the Applicant’s claims of fear of persecution and the risk of harm.

claim: Claims of non-refoulement protection (protection against being returned to a country where they may face persecution or harm) for themselves and their children, based on risk of persecution and harm due to A1's conversion from Islam to Christianity and A4's rejection of a suitor in the Philippines.
requested_remedy: Claims of non-refoulement protection (protection against being returned to a country where they may face persecution or harm) for themselves and their children, based on risk of persecution and harm due to A1's conversion from Islam to Christianity and A4's rejection of a suitor in the Philippines.
parties: Plaintiff: A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, and A6 (a family consisting of a Pakistani husband, his Filipino wife, and their four children)

facts.F1: A1, the husband, was born and raised as a Muslim in Pakistan, but converted to Christianity while in Hong Kong.
facts.F2: A1's conversion led to his family's disownment and a report being filed against him for blasphemy in Pakistan.
facts.F3: A4, the wife, rejected a suitor in the Philippines, who had threatened her and their eldest son.
facts.F4: The family members have been released on recognizance, pending the determination of their claims.
facts.F5: Their non-refoulement claims were separately considered and determined by the Director of Immigration and rejected.
facts.F6: Their appeals to the Torture Claims Appeal Board (Board) were consolidated and dismissed.
facts.F7: A1 was arrested and convicted multiple times in Hong Kong for various offenses, including overstaying, indecent assault, and theft.
facts.F8: A1 and A4 have been arrested and repatriated to their home countries in the past.
facts.F9: A4 worked as a foreign domestic helper in Hong Kong and met A1, with whom she formed a relationship.
facts.F10: Their children were born in Hong Kong or the Philippines.
facts.F11: A1's conversion and A4's rejection of the suitor have led to threats and fear of persecution and harm in their home countries.
facts.F12: The Adjudicator in the Board's decision made relevant findings that were considered by the court.
facts.F13: The court considered the country guidance that Christian converts in Pakistan are at a greater risk of persecution due to charges of apostasy and blasphemy.

lawsuit_type: Application for Leave to Apply for Judicial Review
reference_issues: Whether the Board's decision was unreasonable and/or irrational in assessing A1's risk as a Christian convert in Pakistan.
Whether the Board erred in law in requiring A1 to produce corroborating evidence for his claim for non-refoulement protection.
Whether the Board failed to properly and separately assess the claims of the minor children, particularly their sons A5 and A6.
authorities:
Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance, Cap 383 (HKBOR)
1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees
Section 2.4 and 2.5 of the UKBA Country Policy and Information Note Pakistan: Christians and Christian Converts Guidance, September 2018

Fabio Arlyn Timogan [2021] 2 HKC 458

claim: The applicant claimed that she would be at risk of harm if she was refouled to Vietnam, due to a debt dispute with a creditor and threats to her life.
requested_remedy: The applicant claimed that she would be at risk of harm if she was refouled to Vietnam, due to a debt dispute with a creditor and threats to her life.
parties: Defendant: The Director of Immigration/ The Torture Claims Appeal Board/ Non-refoulement Claims Petition Office

facts.F1: The applicant is a national of Vietnam, born in 1982.
facts.F2: She entered Hong Kong illegally in April 2011 and was removed by the Immigration Department in September of the same year.
facts.F3: She entered Hong Kong again in February 2013 lawfully and was granted extension of stay until 1 April 2014, but overstayed since then.
facts.F4: She was arrested on 19 March 2014 and sentenced to 2 months' imprisonment for breach of condition of stay.
facts.F5: She was later released on recognizance.
facts.F6: In May 2015, she was arrested again and convicted of offences including taking up unlawful employment and sentenced to 22 months' imprisonment.
facts.F7: The applicant lodged a non-refoulement claim to the Immigration Department on 3 July 2014, claiming that she would be harmed or killed by her creditor if refouled to Vietnam.
facts.F8: She claimed that she had borrowed 600 million Vietnamese Dong from her creditor in 2012 for her business in a poultry farm and failed to repay the debt since November 2012.
facts.F9: She reported to the police but they did not follow up the matter.
facts.F10: She later came to know a man from Hong Kong, Ah Sum, and they completed their marriage procedure in Vietnam, and she left Vietnam for Hong Kong on 27 February 2013.
facts.F11: The Director of Immigration rejected the applicant's non-refoulement claim on all applicable grounds on 7 July 2016 and 10 January 2017.
facts.F12: The applicant lodged an appeal/petition to the Torture Claims Appeal Board/Non-refoulement Claims Petition Office against the Director's second decision dated 10 January 2017.
facts.F13: The Board dismissed the appeal on 17 January 2019, finding that there was no evidence to show that the applicant would be at risk of harm if refouled to Vietnam.
facts.F14: The applicant's claims were considered weak, with bare assertions without details and evidence in support.
facts.F15: The applicant did not provide sufficient evidence to support her claims of threat and risk of harm.

lawsuit_type: Application for Leave to Apply for Judicial Review
reference_issues: Whether the applicant would be at risk of harm if refouled to Vietnam due to a debt dispute with a creditor and threats to her life

Whether the Director of Immigration and the Torture Claims Appeal Board/Non-refoulement Claims Petition Office properly assessed the risk of harm and the availability of state protection and internal relocation
authorities:
Part VIIC of the Immigration Ordinance, Cap 115 (non-refoulement protection)
BOR 2, BOR 3, persecution risk, and torture risk (applicable grounds for non-refoulement claims)
relevant_cases:
Nupur Mst v Director of Immigration [2018] HKCA 524 (principles regarding appeals on non-refoulement cases)
ST v Betty Kwan [2014] 4 HKLRD 277 (no absolute right to an oral hearing)

claim: Claim of non-refoulement
requested_remedy: Claim of non-refoulement
parties: Defendant: ['Torture Claims Appeal Board/Non-refoulement Claims Petition Office', 'Director of Immigration']

facts.F1: The applicant, a Bangladeshi national, entered Hong Kong illegally and was arrested on 28 June 2014.
facts.F2: The applicant raised a non-refoulement claim with the Director of Immigration on 1 July 2014.
facts.F3: The applicant claimed that if he were to be returned to Bangladesh, he would be harmed or killed by Mohammad Ramzan and the Awami League members and the Muslim people in his village.
facts.F4: The applicant was a member of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party and was involved in a fight with the Awami League in 2011, and was beaten up in 2012 and threatened in 2014.
facts.F5: The applicant is a Hindu and claimed to have suffered discrimination because of his religion.
facts.F6: The Director of Immigration considered the applicant's non-refoulement claim under various provisions, including Part VIIC of the Immigration Ordinance, Cap. 115, Article 2 of Section 8 of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance, Cap. 383, Article 3 of section 8 of the HKBOR, and the non-refoulement principle under Article 33 of the 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees and its 1967 Protocol.
facts.F7: The Director refused the applicant's non-refoulement claim on 10 January 2017.
facts.F8: The applicant appealed to the Torture Claims Appeal Board/Non-refoulement Claims Petition Office, which re-heard the case and refused the applicant's appeal on 27 July 2018.
facts.F9: The applicant applied for leave to apply for judicial review of the Board's Decision on 8 August 2018.
facts.F10: The applicant claimed that the Director and the Board failed to exercise their discretion fairly and reasonably, and failed to meet the greater care and duty owed to a self-represented claimant.
facts.F11: The applicant also claimed that the Hearing Bundle was given to him shortly before the appeal hearing, and that he was not given sufficient time to prepare, and that the Bundle was in English without translation.
facts.F12: However, the applicant later confirmed that he had no complaint against the Adjudicator and that the appeal hearing was a fair hearing.
facts.F13: The applicant also admitted that he had assistance with the Hearing Bundle before the appeal hearing and understood its content.
facts.F14: No evidence supported that the Director and the Board failed to exercise their discretion fairly and reasonably.
facts.F15: The applicant's claims regarding the Hearing Bundle were inconsistent with his evidence in court.
facts.F16: The applicant could not identify which part of the Country of Origin Information was outdated or hearsay.

lawsuit_type: Application for Leave to Apply for Judicial Review
reference_issues: Whether the Director and the Board failed to exercise their discretion fairly and reasonably.
Whether the applicant was given sufficient time to prepare for the appeal hearing.
Whether the Hearing Bundle was in a language that the applicant could understand.
Whether the Board relied on outdated or hearsay Country of Origin Information.
authorities:
Part VIIC of the Immigration Ordinance, Cap. 115 (Torture risk)
Article 2 of Section 8 of the Hong Kong Bill of Rights Ordinance, Cap. 383 (Risk of violation of the right to life)
Article 3 of section 8 of the HKBOR (Risk of torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment)
Article 33 of the 1951 Convention relating to the Status of Refugees and its 1967 Protocol (Persecution risk under RC)
